reason: The sources provide sufficient details to support a surprising 45-second story with well over 10 validated claims.
story: In 1958, astrophysicist Eugene Parker used just four lines of algebra to prove something radical: the Sun's million-degree atmosphere, the corona, is simply too hot to stay put. He predicted that gravity weakens enough with distance to launch a relentless, supersonic river of plasma tearing through the solar system at a million miles per hour. When he submitted his groundbreaking paper to The Astrophysical Journal, reviewers mocked it as utter nonsense and recommended rejection. One reviewer even suggested Parker go to the library and read up on the subject first. But the journal's editor bravely overruled them and published it anyway. Just one year later, Soviet spacecraft Luna 1 directly detected the wind, and Mariner 2 confirmed it. Today, we know this solar wind shapes planetary magnetospheres, strips atmospheres, and is finally being touched up close by the very spacecraft named in Parker's honor.
angle: Astrophysicist Eugene Parker's theoretical discovery of the solar wind was rejected by peer reviewers who called it 'utter nonsense,' only to be proven right by spacecraft just one year later.

claims.claim: Eugene Parker published his theoretical paper predicting the solar wind in 1958.
Parker calculated his theory using just four lines of algebra.
Two reviewers of Parker's 1958 paper recommended its rejection, with one calling it utter nonsense.
Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar, the journal editor, overruled the reviewers and published Parker's paper.
The Soviet spacecraft Luna 1 directly observed the solar wind in January 1959.
The solar corona reaches temperatures of over a million degrees Celsius or Kelvin.
The solar wind travels at speeds up to a million miles per hour (or roughly 400 to 800-1000 kilometers per second).
NASA's Mariner 2 spacecraft confirmed the solar wind observations three years after Luna 1.
The solar wind is composed primarily of protons, electrons, alpha particles, and trace heavy ions.
NASA launched the Parker Solar Probe in 2018, naming it after the living Eugene Parker.
Ludwig Biermann previously postulated a continuous stream of particles to explain the tails of comets pointing away from the Sun.
The solar wind causes geomagnetic storms and auroras when interacting with Earth's magnetosphere.

disputed: Exact historical priority regarding who first suggested the concept of corpuscular radiation or charged streams (ranging from Kepler and Carrington to Eddington, Birkeland, and Lindemann) is framed through multiple historical accounts and should be attributed accordingly rather than credited to a single individual.
